title: HPDT Phar16/367P — Geoffrey Clifford Allen (Pharmacists)
text:
BEFORE THE HEALTH PRACTITIONERS
DISCIPLINARY
HPDT NO:
UNDER
IN THE MATTER
BETWEEN
AND
HEARING held in Wellington on 23 November 2016
TRIBUNAL: Mr K Johnston QC (Chair), Ms
Drake and Mr K Govind
(Members)
IN ATTENDANCE: Ms D Gainey (Executive
Officer)
Ms K O’Brien (Stenographer)
APPEARANCES: Ms M Neill for the Professional
Level 6, 80 The Terrace, Wellington 6011
PO Box 10509, The Terrace, Wellington 6143, New Zealand
Telephone: 64 4 381 6816 Facsimile: 64 4 381 6770
Email: gfraser@hpdt.org.nz

TRIBUNAL
871/Phar16/367P
the Health Practitioners
Competence Assurance Act 2003
of disciplinary charges against a
health practitioner under Part 4 of
the Act
A PROFESSIONAL
CONDUCT COMMITTEE
appointed by THE PHARMACY
COUNCIL OF NEW
ZEALAND
Applicant
GEOFFREY CLIFFORD
ALLEN of New Plymouth,
Pharmacist
Practitioner
L Carlyon, Ms J Dawson, Ms S
Conduct Committee

3
Ms E Wilson for the Practitioner

2
Introduction
1. The Pharmacy Council of New Zealand’s Professional Conduct Committee prefers a
charge against Geoffrey Clifford Allen of New Plymouth, Pharmacist, pursuant to s
100(1)(c) of the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003.
2. Section 100(1)(c) provides:
“1. The Tribunal may make any 1 or more of the orders authorised by
section 101 [the penalties which may be imposed by the Tribunal on a
practitioner in the event of an adverse finding] if, after conducting a
hearing on a charge laid under section 91 against a health practitioner,
it makes 1 or more findings that:
…
(c) the practitioner has been convicted of an offence that reflects
adversely on his or her fitness to practise; or
…
2 The Tribunal may make a finding under sub-section 1(c) only if the
conviction concerned:
…
(b) has been entered by any court in New Zealand or elsewhere for
an offence punishable by imprisonment for a term of 3 months or
longer.”
3. The PCC’s Notice of Charge is dated 30 August 2016, and particularises the charge in
these terms:
“Charge
1 On 10 December 2015, Mr Allen was convicted in the District Court at
New Plymouth of 17 charges pursuant to section 131A (offences
relating to possession of objectionable publications and involving
knowledge) of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act
1993 (the convictions).
2 The convictions, both jointly and severally, reflect adversely on Mr
Allen’s fitness to practise as a pharmacist.

3
3 Each of the convictions were for an offence punishable by
imprisonment for a term of five years.
Particulars
4 A Certified Copy or Extract of the Permanent Court Record,
confirming the conviction of Mr Allen on each of the offences outlined
in the Charge, together with the sentence imposed, is attached.”
4. The primary evidence before the Tribunal was an agreed statement of facts, and we set
this out in full:
“1 Introduction
1.1 Mr Geoffrey Clifford Allen is a 62 year old pharmacist. He gained registration
as a pharmacist in New Zealand on 13 July 1976.
1.2 Mr Allen owned and operated Fitzroy Pharmacy, located at 552 Devon St,
East Fitzroy, New Plymouth (the Pharmacy) for 14 years prior to June 2014.
(Agreed bundle of documents (ABD), tab 2, p 5) Mr Allen was also the
resident pharmacist at the Pharmacy between June 2014 and October 2015.
1.3 Mr Allen has not worked as a pharmacist since October 2015. He currently
works in garden maintenance on a part-time basis, for minimum wage.
2 Background of offending
2.1 The circumstances regarding the offending are set out in the Police summary
of facts (ABD, tab 2) and the sentencing notes of Judge Sygrove (ABD, tab 3).
2.2 The Police were notified by an employee of the Pharmacy’s document
destruction service that over a period of 10 years images containing
objectionable and abusive material had been printed and disposed of from the
Pharmacy by Mr Allen.
2.3 As a result of that notification, Police uplifted images from the document
destruction employee. In particular, hard copy pictures of children or young
persons engaged in, or sufficiently proximate to, sexual connection with other
children or young persons and or adults were obtained.
2.4 Mr Allen’s position at the Pharmacy meant that he would often be the last
person to leave the Pharmacy premises.

4
2.5 After other employees had left, Mr Allen would go into the office at the
Pharmacy and access the Pharmacy’s computer and printer. Mr Allen would
use an internet browser to search for and view objectionable images. He
would then print a number of the images. Mr Allen would then store these
printed images behind a cupboard in the Pharmacy office until disposing of
them in the rubbish.
2.6 By his estimate, Mr Allen would print and store up to approximately 12
images, two or three times a week.
2.7 As part of the Police investigation, Mr Allen was interviewed by the Police. In
his first interview, Mr Allen denied any knowledge of the images seized by
Police. However, Mr Allen subsequently contacted the Police and on or about
16 July 2015 he was re-interviewed by the Police. At this interview, Mr Allen
admitted knowledge and possession of the objectionable material that had
been provided to the Police.
2.8 On 14 July 2015, a search warrant pursuant to the Films, Videos and
Publications Classification Act 1993 was executed at Mr Allen’s home
address. The Police did not find any images at his home address, but seized a
large number of items from Mr Allen’s bedroom including a computer drive
box, hard drives, and USB storage devices. The Police returned Mr Allen’s
personal devices to him in or around February 2016.
3 Conviction
3.1 Mr Allen was charged with 17 counts of possession of objectionable
publications relating to the exploitation of children between 1 January 2014
and 24 June 2014. The 17 charges were pursuant to section 131A of the
Films, Videos, and Publications Classification Act 1993. (ABD, tab 4) There
were 17 images put before the District Court. (ABD, tab 2, p 1 and tab 3, p 1).
3.2 Mr Allen pleaded guilty to all charges at an early stage. (ABD, tab 3, p11 and
tab 4, p 18 – 22)
3.3 Mr Allen appeared before Judge Sygrove in the District Court at New
Plymouth on 10 December 2015. (ABD, tab 3) Mr Allen was sentenced to
seven months home detention. (ABD, tab 4, p 18 – 22)

5
3.4 This is Mr Allen’s first conviction, and first appearance before the Tribunal.”
5. The parties also provided the Tribunal with an Agreed Bundle of Documents.
6. This included the Police Summary of Facts in the criminal proceedings, the District
Court Judge’s sentencing notes, a certified copy of the relevant entry in the criminal
record and correspondence from Wellstop from which organisation the Practitioner has
received counselling.
Liability
7. There is no contest as to liability, the parties being in agreement that the PCC is able to
establish a breach of s 101(1) (c) on the bases that the Practitioner had been convicted
of offences punishable by imprisonment for more than three months, and that his
offending reflects adversely on his fitness to practise.
8. Whilst it is axiomatic that the Tribunal must reach its own conclusions as to liability,
we have had little difficulty in this case reaching the same conclusion as the parties.
The fact of the Practitioner’s convictions is established. Offences under the relevant
provisions of the Films, Videos, and Publications Classifications Act 1993 carry
penalties well in excess of those required by s 100 (2). The only possible area of debate
is whether the Practitioner’s behaviour reflects adversely on his fitness to practise.
Frankly, that question only needs to be posed to be answered. For any health
practitioner to commit indecency offences of this sort reflects adversely on his or her
fitness to practise.
Penalty
9. As was accepted by both parties, the real issue here concerns the appropriate penalty.
10. Ms Neill for the PCC submitted that the appropriate penalty was a censure and the
cancellation of the Practitioner’s registration. Ms Wilson for the Practitioner argued
that a more appropriate penalty would be censure, a period of suspension and the
imposition of conditions on his practising certificate from the date of his re-entry into
the profession designed effectively to ensure his ongoing fitness to practise.
11. Counsel helpfully provided us with detailed submissions as to the principles which
govern the determination of appropriate penalties in professional disciplinary
proceedings. Ms Neill and Ms Wilson’s submissions largely mirrored each other in
this regard. The principles are well settled. We summarise them as follows:

6
• In approaching penalty, the Tribunal must consider all available options;
• Before imposing any particular penalty or combination of penalties, the
Tribunal must satisfy itself that any less severe penalty or combination of
penalties will not meet the case;
• The primary purposes of professional disciplinary proceedings, and the
purposes which the Tribunal must therefore bring to its consideration in any
given case, are the protection of the public and the maintenance of professional
standards;
• Professional disciplinary proceedings are not primarily concerned with
punishment, so that whilst the imposition of any penalty will be punitive,
punishment is not to be an objective;
• The Tribunal is obliged to have regard to the prospects of a practitioner’s
rehabilitation;
• Consistency is important, and the Tribunal must therefore have regard to
penalties imposed in comparable cases in the past. This principle is not to
operate as a straight-jacket. Times change, and societal attitudes with them.
The Tribunal must be free to change its approach. However, it must do so
expressly, and on a principled basis;
• The Tribunal’s responsibility is to identify the least punitive outcome which
meets the seriousness of the practitioner’s conduct;
• In the end, the search is for a penalty which is fair, proportionate and reasonable.
12. For the PCC, Ms Neill’s starting point was that pharmacists provide essential services
within their communities, and the public is entitled to expect them to adhere to a high
standard of conduct. In this regard, she referred us to the Tribunal’s decision in Y
(HPDT 321/Med10/149P) in which the Tribunal said that “The public needs to be
assured that members of their profession who treat them, are practitioners of good
character and good standing in the community. A conviction for possession of
objectionable material does not put the practitioner in such a category.”

7
13. She submitted that the Practitioner’s conduct in this case demonstrated a disregard of
his legal, professional and moral responsibilities of such a degree that it seriously
undermined the profession’s reputation.
14. In developing that submission, Ms Neill emphasised the following:
• The Practitioner was the responsible pharmacist in the pharmacy;
• The conduct occurred in the pharmacy, using the pharmacy’s office equipment;
• The conduct was deliberate and premeditated;
• The type of conduct involved appears to have occurred over a period of years. In
this regard, we mention that the convictions which are before us are in respect of
the Practitioner’s conduct during the first half of 2014 only. Nevertheless, we
accept that there is evidence that the conduct occurred on earlier occasions;
• The Practitioner estimated that he had viewed, printed and stored images two or
three times a week over a sustained period of time;
• The images involved were at the more serious end of the spectrum;
• The victims were children and therefore peculiarly vulnerable.
15. Ms Neill drew our attention to aspects of the Pharmacy Code Conduct of Ethics,
particularly principle 6 which requires pharmacists to “… act in a manner that promotes
public trust and confidence in pharmacists and enhances the reputation of the
profession…”
16. She submitted that an order censuring the Practitioner and ordering his deregistration
would be consistent with previous decisions, and she referred us to a number of those
decisions.1 None relate to pharmacists. They concern doctors and nurses. We do not
propose to offer a detailed analysis of all of the cases to which Ms Neill referred us.
Their broad thrust seems clear enough. In all of these cases the Tribunal made it clear
that serious breaches of the relevant provisions of the Films, Videos and Publications
Act will almost invariably result in deregistration or a period of suspension.
17. Curiously, it is only in cases where the Tribunal was dealing with doctors that it
imposed periods of suspension. All the cases in which the Tribunal was dealing with
nurses resulted in deregistration. It is not obvious to us that the factual situations in
1 Beardsmore (HPDT 2043/Nur09/117P); Lockett (HPDT 246/Nur9/118P); Derecourt (HPDT 14/Nur05/06P);
Joseph (HPDT 506/Med12/228)); R (HPDT) 681/Med14/295P); Y (HPDT 321/Med10/149P); and Dunkley
(HPDT 368/Med11/175P)

8
these cases explain these outcomes. They may however be explained by the personal
circumstances of the practitioners involved; different perceptions on the part of the
Tribunal as to the prospects of rehabilitation for example.
18. Certainly the Tribunal as currently constituted does not accept that there are any
different expectations of doctors and nurses, or that those same expectations do not
apply equally to pharmacists.
19. In any event, Ms Neill’s submission was that these decisions “… demonstrate that the
Tribunal treats decisions where health practitioners have been convicted of or engaged
in conduct in relating to sexual exploitation of children in publications very seriously
and worthy of severe penalty. This is not only to indicate the Tribunal’s condemnation
of such behaviour, but to also uphold professional standards by sending a strong
message to deter practitioners from engaging in conduct such as this which badly
erodes the public’s confidence in the profession…”
20. Ms Neill acknowledged that the Practitioner had voluntarily undertaken a six-month
treatment programme since his conviction, and that those administering the programme
had provided some supporting evidence and offered the view that the risk of him
reoffending was low.
21. Ms Neill concluded her submissions by re-emphasising the PCC’s submission that this
was a case in which the Tribunal would be justified in censuring and deregistering the
Practitioner, submitting that such an outcome would be fair, proportionate and
reasonable in the circumstances.
22. For the Practitioner, Ms Wilson commenced her submissions for the Practitioner in
relation to penalty by contending that “… his use of pornography was borne out of
[dysfunction] in his personal relationships. He initially accessed adult images, but then
stumbled across images featuring children. He then habitually accessed these images
approximately two to three times per week…” Generally, such a submission would
have to be grounded on expert evidence. However, the Tribunal is prepared to accept
that the Practitioner’s dysfunctional personal life may have played a part in his
offending.
23. She then submitted that the Practitioner’s “…offending did not involve any others, and
was limited to accessing the images only; he did not distribute or save any images.
Rather the images were printed in hard copy, and then discarded of in a document
destruction bin…” Of course it is not correct to say that the offending did not involve

9
others; it certainly involved the children who were the subject of the images. But, the
Tribunal accepts that the point Ms Wilson’s submission was directed at was that there
is no evidence suggesting that the Practitioner shared the images with anyone else.
24. Ms Wilson then made the point that although he initially denied the charge brought
against him in the criminal proceeding, ultimately, he took responsibility for his
conduct, approached the Police and confessed.
25. She then emphasised that the Practitioner has since undergone counselling and that
those responsible for his counselling describe him as showing good insight into his
conduct, significant remorse, and assess him as being at low risk of reoffending.
26. Ms Wilson informed us that, as a direct result of his conduct, the Practitioner’s marriage
has broken up, that he has lost his home and his job and now has only limited contact
with his children and no contact with his grandchildren. He is currently working part-
time as a labourer at a garden centre.
27. Focusing specifically on the appropriate penalty in this case Ms Wilson reminded us
that the Practitioner is 63 years old, has practised for 38 years, has no criminal or
professional disciplinary record and that there is no evidence to suggest that he is
anything other than a competent and experienced pharmacist.
28. She said that despite his initial denial of any wrong-doing he has adopted a responsible
attitude to both the criminal charges and this professional disciplinary charge. The
Tribunal accepts that, and acknowledges that the Practitioner is entitled to credit for
doing so.
29. She re-emphasised that the Practitioner “… shows excellent insight into his offending,
and has done from an early stage. The District Court noted in its sentencing decision
that that [the Practitioner] had demonstrated clear insight and remorse, having
engaged with counselling…” She also re-emphasised the most recent reports from the
organisation providing counselling services to the Practitioner all of which, as the
Tribunal has already indicated, are positive.
30. Ms Wilson told us that the Practitioner accepts that his offending was not victimless,
and in this regard acknowledges the harm that this pernicious trade in pornography
causes to the children involved, as well as the harm he has caused to his wife and family.
31. She then went on to say that the Practitioner “… is now forward thinking. He is working
again (as a labourer) and is hopeful for some work doing-up old houses. He does not
have any particular plans to work in pharmacy, but would like to retain the option to

10
do so. He has achieved much in the time that he has been in counselling, which he
continues to attend…”
32. She re-emphasised the devastating impact that the Practitioner’s conduct had had on his
own life, with the break-up of his marriage and the limited contact he now has with his
children. As a result of these things she described him as being extremely motivated,
and told the Tribunal that “… he will not reoffend…”
33. Turning to comparable cases, Ms Wilson accepted that “… generally cases involving
possession of objectionable material result in suspension or cancellation. It appears
that a major factor in sentence selection is the level of insight and potential for
rehabilitation shown by the Practitioner…”
34. Understandably, in this context, Ms Wilson focused on those cases (which all happen
to be cases involving doctors), in which the outcome did not involve cancellation of
registration. Thus she focused on Joseph and Y. These cases she contrasted with R
where, as she submitted, the Tribunal had no evidence as to the practitioner’s risk of
reoffending. Although she did not put it in quite these terms, the Tribunal’s
understanding of the submission is that that is the major difference between Joseph and
Y on the one hand where the Tribunal did not feel it necessary to cancel the doctor’s
registration, and R on the other hand where it did.
35. Ms Wilson then submitted that this case was more akin to Joseph and Y, precisely
because such evidence as there is here indicates that the Practitioner’s chances of
reoffending are low and that there is reasonable prospects of his rehabilitation which
she submitted “… translates to a corresponding low risk to the public…”. On that
basis, Ms Wilson submitted that “…cancellation would simply be too high a penalty.”
36. Finally, Ms Wilson submitted that an appropriate penalty in this case would be a
censure, suspension for a period of nine months and the imposition of conditions on his
return to practise.
Discussion
37. The Tribunal is indebted to Ms Wilson for putting the Practitioner’s case in the clearest
possible terms. She said everything that could possibly have been said on his behalf.
However, we do not accept the submission that censure and cancellation would, to use
Ms Wilson’s expression, “… simply be too high a penalty…”
38. We have reached the conclusion in this case that we cannot discharge our
responsibilities to the public and the profession as earlier described without censuring

11
the Practitioner and cancelling his registration. That, we emphasise, is a conclusion we
have only been able to reach after considering the other realistic option put to us on the
Practitioner’s behalf by Ms Wilson that we censure the Practitioner, suspend his
registration and impose conditions on him which would apply if and when he re-entered
the profession. In short, it appears to the Tribunal that censure and deregistration is the
fair, proportionate and reasonable penalty here.
39. In reaching that conclusion we have regard to six key points:
(i) The Practitioner’s offending was extremely serious;
(ii) Whilst the criminal offending with which we are dealing relates to offences
committed during the first half of 2014, the Practitioner himself admits that his
offending took place over some years;
(iii) The seriousness of the offending, and his breach of his legal, professional and
moral obligations, not only calls into question the Practitioner’s fitness to
practice, but, inevitably, has brought disrepute to the pharmacy profession as a
whole.
(iv) There is an important public safety aspect to this case. Counsels’ submissions
on this tended to focus on different points. Ms Neill for the PCC submitted that
the public safety issue was the perception that the public would have of how the
Practitioner’s conduct was addressed by the profession. Ms Wilson for the
Practitioner focused on the issue of whether the Practitioner presents a threat to
future patients. It is in the former sense that the Tribunal has concluded that the
protection of the public must be considered. We doubt whether the Practitioner
presents a direct threat. But our perception is that if the Practitioner were
permitted to retain his registration in the face of these convictions, the public’s
confidence in the profession would be seriously compromised;
(v) The Tribunal is prepared to accept that, behind the Practitioner’s offending,
there were difficult personal circumstances with which he was dealing (even
although there is no direct evidence to support this contention). In the absence
of any evidence as to the precise nature of these circumstances and their impact
on the Practitioner, we cannot take this point any further;
(vi) The Tribunal accepts that the Practitioner is entitled to credit for his years of
service to the profession and his hitherto unblemished record. Indeed, these
factors caused us some difficulty in reaching the conclusion that we have. In

12
the end, however, the seriousness of the Practitioner’s breach of the legal,
professional and moral standards to which the public is entitled to expect
pharmacists to adhere, and the demands of the protection of the public and the
maintenance of professional standards outweighed these considerations.
Costs
40. The costs issue in professional disciplinary proceedings is fraught. The question is
always the proportion of the costs involved in such proceedings which should be borne
by the profession itself, all the members of which derive a benefit from the existence of
robust professional disciplinary regime, and the proportion which should be borne by
the Practitioner who, at least in cases where misconduct has been established, is
responsible for those costs being incurred in the first place.
41. Approaches vary across professional disciplines. In some professions, the starting point
is that the practitioner is expected to pay 100% of the costs involved unless there are
good and proper reasons for moving from that position. In most professional groups,
health practitioners included, the starting point is that the Practitioner is expected to
contribute 50% of those costs unless the circumstances require otherwise.
42. Here, the PCC seeks the usual order for 50% of the costs involved.
43. We record that the Tribunal’s costs in this matter total $11,813.76, and that those of the
PCC total $10,000.
44. One of the circumstances which can lead the Tribunal to vary the usual 50% order is
the financial circumstances of the practitioner involved. Here, Ms Wilson produced
without objection an affidavit sworn by the Practitioner which indicates essentially that
he has no assets, liabilities of fractionally over $30,000 and an income of just over $400
per week which barely covers his weekly expenses. In short, he is insolvent. Ms Wilson
submits with some force that in the circumstances no costs order should be made as
there is no realistic prospect of any such order being paid.
45. The Tribunal is reluctant to make an order which is never likely to be enforceable and
which will almost inevitably lead to his bankruptcy. Those things said, we think that
there is a case for a nominal costs award in favour of the PCC which the Practitioner
may have some prospect of paying in the foreseeable future and would at least mean
that he had made some contribution to the costs of this proceeding.
46. We will make an order that the Practitioner pay $500 on account of the PCC’s costs.

13
Conclusion
47. The Tribunal’s formal orders follow:
46.1 Pursuant to s101(1)(d) of the health
2003, the Tribunal censures the
Practitioner;
46.2 Pursuant to s101(1)(a), the Tribunal
orders
cancelled;
46.3 Pursuant to s101(1)(f), the Tribunal
account of the PCC’s costs;
46.4 Pursuant to s157, the Tribunal directs
this decision, and a summary, on the
